findings.rationale: Admin authorization is decided purely client-side from the `role` claim of a JWT that is base64-decoded without any signature or issuer verification. A user can craft/replace the token in the store (e.g. via devtools or a tampered login response) and set role='admin' to pass the guard; expiry (`exp`) is also never checked. Access control must be enforced server-side on every protected request.

readClaims decodes the JWT payload with atob/JSON.parse and returns it as trusted TokenClaims without validating the signature, algorithm, or expiry. Returning these as authoritative claims invites their use for security decisions (as done in AuthService.isAdmin). It also throws on malformed tokens (no try/catch, unchecked split index).

The route guard grants access to admin routes solely on the client-evaluated isAdmin() result derived from unverified token data; bypassing the guard (or tampering with the token) exposes admin routes and any data they load if the backend does not re-check permissions.

displayName() decodes the JWT payload client-side with readClaims() without any signature/expiry verification. Here it only feeds a display string (the real admin decision is delegated to the server via /api/me), so impact is limited to spoofed/UI-injected identity text, but relying on unverified token claims is a fragile pattern that must never be extended to access decisions.

readClaims blindly splits, base64-decodes and JSON.parses attacker-controllable token content with no structural validation or try/catch; a malformed token throws an unhandled exception (and the returned claims are trusted as TokenClaims without checking the fields exist).

The admin decision is made entirely on the client from an unverified JWT payload: the token is base64-decoded without any signature or issuer validation, so a user can craft/modify a token (e.g. via TokenStore.set or by tampering with the token source) with role='admin' and a future exp to pass the guard and reach admin routes/UI. Authorization must be enforced server-side; client claim inspection may only be a UX hint.

readClaims() parses the JWT payload with atob/JSON.parse and returns it as trusted TokenClaims without verifying the signature, algorithm, issuer or audience. Returning these attacker-controllable values as authoritative claims is what enables the privilege escalation in adminGuard; it also throws on malformed tokens (unhandled parse error).
